content: One of the most pivotal statutes in shaping the modern American pharmaceutical market was the 1984 Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act, commonly referred to as the Hatch-Waxman Act, named after its primary sponsors. 3. The Hatch-Waxman Act was designed to address two problematic interactions: the new regulations mandated by the 1962 amendments and the existing patent law, which is regulated by the United States Patent and Trademark Office rather than the FDA. 4. The additional clinical trials required by the 1962 amendments caused significant delays in the marketing of new drugs, without extending the duration of the manufacturer’s patent. This led to a reduced period of market exclusivity for pioneer drug manufacturers, impacting their profitability. 5. Conversely, the new regulations could be interpreted as requiring full safety and efficacy testing for generic versions of approved drugs. Court decisions obtained by pioneer manufacturers prevented generic manufacturers from initiating clinical trials while the original drug was still under patent. 6. The Hatch-Waxman Act was intended as a compromise between pioneer and generic drug manufacturers. It aimed to lower the overall cost of bringing generics to market, thereby reducing long-term drug prices, while preserving the profitability of developing new drugs. 7. The Act extended the patent exclusivity terms for new drugs and linked these extensions, in part, to the length of the FDA approval process for each individual drug. 8. For generic manufacturers, the Act introduced a new approval mechanism called the Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA). This allowed generic manufacturers to demonstrate that their formulation had the same active ingredient, route of administration, dosage form, strength, and pharmacokinetic properties (bioequivalence) as the corresponding brand-name drug. 9. The Hatch-Waxman Act is widely credited with establishing the modern generic drug industry. 10. During the early AIDS epidemic, concerns about the length of the drug approval process became a prominent issue. 11. In the mid-to-late 1980s, HIV activist organizations like ACT-UP accused the FDA of unnecessarily delaying the approval of medications for HIV and opportunistic infections. They staged large protests, including a confrontational action at the FDA campus on October 11, 1988, which resulted in nearly 180 arrests. 12. In August 1990, Dr. Louis Lasagna, then chairman of a presidential advisory panel on drug approval, estimated that thousands of lives were lost annually due to delays in the approval and marketing of drugs for cancer and AIDS. 13. In response to these criticisms, the FDA implemented new rules to expedite the approval of drugs for life-threatening diseases and expanded pre-approval access to drugs for patients with limited treatment options. 14. The first of these new rules was the IND exemption or treatment IND rule, which allowed expanded access to a drug undergoing Phase II or III trials (or, in extraordinary cases, even earlier) if it potentially represented a safer or better alternative to existing treatments for terminal or serious illnesses. 15. A second new rule, the parallel track policy, permitted drug companies to establish mechanisms for access to a new potentially life-saving drug by patients who, for various reasons, could not participate in ongoing clinical trials. 16. The parallel track designation could be made at the time of IND submission. 17. The accelerated approval rules were further expanded and codified in 1992. 18. All of the initial drugs approved for the treatment of HIV/AIDS were approved through accelerated approval mechanisms. 19. For example, a treatment IND was issued for the first HIV drug, AZT, in 1985, and it was approved just two years later in 1987. 20. Three of the first five drugs targeting HIV were approved in the United States before they were approved in any other country. 21. An ongoing court case, Abigail Alliance v. von Eschenbach, has the potential to force significant changes in FDA regulation of unapproved drugs. 22. Abigail Burroughs was a college student diagnosed with head and neck cancer. During the later phases of her treatment, her father sued the FDA for access to the experimental biotechnology drug cetuximab. 23. At that time, cetuximab was only available experimentally for patients participating in colon cancer clinical trials. It has since been approved for colon cancer and head and neck cancer when combined with radiation therapy. 24. The Abigail Alliance argued in court that terminal cancer patients have a Constitutionally protected right to access experimental medications before FDA approval. 25. Specifically, the Abigail Alliance contended that the FDA should license drugs for use by terminally ill patients with desperate diagnoses after they have completed Phase I testing. 26. In May 2006, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled in favor of the Abigail Alliance, finding that the U.S. Constitution protects the right of terminally ill patients to access treatments not yet approved by the FDA. 27. On March 1, 2007, the U.S. Court of Appeals was scheduled to rehear the case at the FDA’s request. 28. This case has the potential to fundamentally alter the conduct of clinical cancer research, as the initial Court of Appeals ruling essentially permits unrestricted access to experimental drugs by terminally ill patients, who would then have little incentive to participate in Phase II and Phase III clinical trials. 29. The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) filed an amicus brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals in advance of the March 1 hearing, supporting the FDA. 30. ASCO argued that the Constitution does not guarantee the right to access unapproved medications and that the court case threatens the integrity of the cancer clinical trial enterprise. 31. The widely publicized recall of Vioxx, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) now estimated to have contributed to fatal heart attacks in thousands of Americans, played a significant role in driving a new wave of safety reforms at both the FDA rulemaking and statutory levels. 32. Vioxx was approved by the FDA in 1999 and was initially hoped to be safer than previous NSAIDs due to its reduced risk of gastrointestinal tract bleeding. 33. However, numerous preand post-marketing studies suggested that Vioxx might increase the risk of myocardial infarction, a finding conclusively demonstrated by results from the APPROVe trial in 2004. 34. Faced with numerous lawsuits, the manufacturer voluntarily withdrew Vioxx from the market. 35. The Vioxx case has been central to an ongoing debate over whether new drugs should be evaluated based on their absolute safety or their safety relative to existing treatments for a given condition. 36. In the wake of the Vioxx recall, there were widespread calls from major newspapers, medical journals, consumer advocacy organizations, lawmakers, and FDA officials for reforms in the FDA’s procedures for preand post-market drug safety regulation. 37. In 2006, a congressionally requested committee was appointed by the Institute of Medicine to review pharmaceutical safety regulation in the U.S. and to issue recommendations for improvements.
